does-a-smaller-box-cut-wfs-fees.html.text:
← Walmart Marketplace calculator

Does a smaller box cut my WFS fee?

Every other decision on this tool trades leftover against take rate — match the Buy Box, run Connect ads, offer 2-day. This one leaves the listing alone. The WFS fulfillment fee is a step function of the carton you ship: its longest, median and shortest sides, and its billable weight. A box that is half an inch over on one side pays a whole tier more on every unit, for as long as you sell it, and nothing on the listing says so.

What Seller Center will not tell you is which measurement is the expensive one. The default 19 × 13 × 7 in carton at 3 lb bills as Oversize at $9.20. It misses Standard on one thing only — the longest side, by 1.00 in. Repacked to 17.5 × 13 × 7 at 2.9 lb it is Standard at $5.35, a $3.85 drop per unit. After $0.35 to repack that is $3.50 a unit, or $420.00 across 120 units a month.

Box Sides (in) Weight Tier Cu ft Fulfillment fee

What is keeping your carton out of Standard

    Standard needs the longest side at or under 18 in, the median at or under 14 in, the shortest at or under 8 in, and weight at or under 20 lb. The three sides are sorted before they are checked, so it does not matter which field you typed each one into.

    Only the fulfillment fee and the repack cost are compared here. Referral, cost of goods and inbound are identical on both sides of a repack, so folding them in would bury a $4 fee step inside a $20 ticket. Complementary to the unit leftover on the main calculator, to WFS vs seller fulfilled (who ships it at all), to aged leftover vs a removal (units already inbound), to 2-day vs WFS, to returns vs WFS, to hold vs match vs promo, and to Walmart Connect vs skip. The tier ceilings and fees here are illustrative defaults — replace them with the figures on your current Seller Center preview before acting on any of it.

    The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend repacking, and it does not tell you a carton is safe to ship.

    Common questions

    Does a smaller box cut Walmart WFS fees?

    Only if it crosses a step. The WFS fulfillment fee is a step function of the longest, median and shortest sides and the billable weight, so shaving a carton that stays inside the same tier and weight band changes nothing. On the calculator defaults a 19 × 13 × 7 in carton at 3 lb bills as Oversize at $9.20. Repacked to 17.5 × 13 × 7 at 2.9 lb it is Standard at $5.35 — $3.85 less per unit. After $0.35 to repack that is $3.50 a unit, or $420.00 across 120 units a month. This page does the arithmetic from the measurements you enter; it does not publish Walmart's live fee schedule.

    Which measurement is keeping my carton out of Standard?

    The page names each one separately. Standard requires the longest side at or under 18 in, the median at or under 14 in, the shortest at or under 8 in, and weight at or under 20 lb. The default 19 × 13 × 7 in carton misses on one thing only — the longest side, by 1.00 in. That is the sentence a fee preview cannot give you, because it shows a single number and not the constraint behind it. The sides are sorted before they are checked, so it does not matter which box you typed length into.

    When is repacking not worth it?

    Three ways, and the page reports each rather than showing a $0.00 saving. A repack that stays in the same tier and band saves nothing, so the labour is a straight loss — shaving the default carton to 18.9 in is still Oversize and costs $42.00 a month. A repack that consolidates units and gains weight can cost more to fulfil, not less. And a real tier drop can still lose: at $5.00 a unit to repack, the $3.85 saving leaves you $1.15 a unit worse, or $138.00 a month. The break-even repack cost on the defaults is $3.85 a unit.

Add a competitive match price to see if that drop still profits. Everything runs in this page; nothing is uploaded.

What this checks

Generic “Walmart seller fee” pages often stop at a referral percentage. The decisions sellers actually face are WFS vs seller fulfilled on the same SKU and whether matching a lower offer still leaves a profit. The referral floor also bites on cheap items. WFS vs seller fulfilled: which path leaves more? walks through that in search-query words. This is not the same job as Walmart's own official fee lookup — this calculator vs. Walmart's WFS Cost Estimator says which one to open for which question, and this calculator vs. a spreadsheet covers what a referral-percentage formula misses. A 2-day Buy Box weight is a further mix: Should I offer 2-day shipping on Walmart? compares WFS (2-day included) against a seller-fulfilled 2-day label and standard shipping after take rate. Returns are a different mix: Should I stay on WFS after Walmart returns? compares expected leftover after a refund, WFS return processing, and the return label you buy. Leftover units already inbound are a further mix: Should I pull aged WFS inventory? compares keeping them under aged storage, paying a removal and selling them yourself, and disposing. Traffic is a further mix: Should I run Walmart Connect ads? compares skipping ads against Sponsored Products after extra units and last-click attribution on organic sales. A lower competing offer is a further mix: Should I match the lower Walmart offer? compares holding the list against a permanent match and a time-boxed promo after Buy Box take. The carton itself is the one lever that leaves the price alone: Does a smaller box cut my WFS fee? compares the box you ship against a repack, names which measurement is over the Standard ceiling and by how much, and nets the repack labour off the fee it saves.

It does not recommend a price, a category, or a fulfillment method, and it is not tax or financial advice. The gap between paths is an arithmetic comparison of the rates you entered.

Common questions

Should I use WFS or seller fulfilled on Walmart Marketplace?

Compare both paths on the same sale price and cost of goods. WFS adds a fulfillment fee, inbound to a Walmart warehouse, and monthly storage. Seller fulfilled replaces those with the shipping label you pay. This page does the arithmetic from the rates you enter; it does not recommend a fulfillment method.

How do I calculate Walmart Marketplace seller fees?

Start with the item price. Subtract the category referral fee (or the per-item minimum if that is larger), then WFS fulfillment and storage if you use WFS, or your own label if you ship. Enter the rates from your current Seller Center fee preview — this page does not publish Walmart's live schedule.

If I have to match a lower Walmart price, do I still make money?

Enter the competitive match price. The calculator re-runs the same costs at that price and shows whether profit stays non-negative. Matching is a common Walmart listing pressure; this is arithmetic, not a pricing recommendation.

Should I buy a 2-day label myself or use WFS?

WFS includes two-day delivery after inbound. A seller-fulfilled 2-day label plus pack time usually converts more than standard shipping and still often loses to WFS once take rate is mixed in. On the defaults WFS keeps $4.83 more per session than an $8.95 2-day label. Open the 2-day page to replace the label, minutes, and take rates from Seller Center.

Do Walmart returns change whether WFS still beats seller fulfilled?

The completed-sale table assumes the order sticks. On the defaults an 8% return mix still leaves seller fulfilled $0.16 ahead per unit ($7.33 vs $7.17) because the $4.50 outbound label plus a $5.50 return label is worse than WFS return processing, but not enough to flip an $0.59 completed-sale gap. At 20% returns WFS keeps $0.49 more. Open the returns page to replace the rate, WFS return fee, and return label from Seller Center.

Should I pull leftover units out of WFS?

Inbound and cost of goods are already spent on leftover units. On the defaults a 12% monthly sell-through over 4 months still leaves a $1.25 removal plus your own label $338.35 ahead of aged WFS storage ($599.66 vs $261.31). Keeping matches at about 41.3% monthly sell-through. Open the aged-inventory page to replace the leftover count, sell-through, aged rate, and removal fee from Seller Center.

Should I run Walmart Connect ads on this listing?

The ads-per-unit line is a completed-sale leftover. On the defaults — 60 organic units, 12 extra ad units, 15% ACOS, and 40% last-click on organic — skipping ads keeps $31.15 more than Sponsored Products ($518.99 vs $487.84). Ads match at about 11.5% ACOS. An 8% ACOS flips ahead by $31.83. Open the ads page to replace ACOS, extra units, and attribution from Ads Manager.

Should I match a lower Walmart offer if it wins more of the Buy Box?

The match field holds take fixed. On the defaults — $21.99 match, 60 completed sales at a 40% hold take, 70% match take, and a 10-day promo at 80% — permanently matching keeps $121.49 more than holding the list ($640.48 vs $518.99). A 10-day promo is $589.99. A 20-day promo flips ahead of the permanent match. Holding matches if match take falls to about 56.7%. Open the Buy Box page to replace the match price and take rates from Seller Center.

should-i-match-the-walmart-buy-box.html.text:
← Walmart Marketplace calculator

Should I match the lower Walmart offer?

Sellers search this after a competing offer undercuts them and the Buy Box moves. The main calculator’s match field is one leftover on a completed sale at the lower ticket, so it cannot show whether the extra take covers that thinner unit. Holding the list keeps today’s leftover at today’s take. Permanently matching sells more of the sessions that already saw the listing, at the lower ticket, every day. A time-boxed promo uses the match ticket at a higher take for N days — before competitors react — then reverts.

On the default $24.99 home unit on WFS, permanently matching $21.99 at 70% take keeps $121.49 more than holding the list at 40% take ($640.48 vs $518.99) on 60 completed sales. A 10-day promo at 80% take is $589.99, $50.50 behind the match. The promo catches a permanent drop at about 17.1 days. Holding matches if match take falls to about 56.7%. A 20-day promo flips ahead of the permanent match by $20.50. A 50% match take and 50% promo take flip the leftover back to holding by $61.50.

Path Price Take Completed Monthly leftover vs hold

Monthly leftover is take% × completed-sale profit × sessions, and sessions are completed sales divided by the hold take. Complementary to the unit-profit match on the main calculator (same take, lower ticket), to WFS vs seller fulfilled (a completed sale), to 2-day vs WFS (fulfillment vs take, price held), to returns vs WFS (a refund, not a price), to aged leftover vs a removal (units already inbound), and to Walmart Connect vs skip (buying traffic, price held). Paste the match price and take rates from your current Seller Center offer. This page does not publish Walmart’s live Buy Box rules.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend holding the list, permanently matching, or running a promo.

Common questions

Should I match a lower Walmart offer to win the Buy Box?

On the calculator defaults — a $24.99 home unit on WFS, 15% referral, $21.99 match, 60 completed sales at a 40% hold take, 70% match take, and a 10-day promo at 80% take — permanently matching keeps $121.49 more than holding the list ($640.48 vs $518.99). A 10-day promo is $589.99, $50.50 behind the match. The promo catches a permanent drop at about 17.1 days. Holding matches if match take falls to about 56.7%. This page does the arithmetic from the rates you enter; it does not recommend a price.

Is this the same as the match price on the main Walmart calculator?

No. The main calculator re-runs the same costs at a lower ticket and holds take fixed, so it cannot show whether winning more of the Buy Box covers the thinner unit. This page mixes take rate with that thinner leftover, and a time-boxed promo that reverts. A completed-sale WFS versus seller table, a 2-day take-rate mix, a refund mix, aged leftover, and Walmart Connect ads are different squeezes.

When does a Walmart promo still beat a permanent match?

When the promo is long enough that its higher take outweighs the days you spend back at the hold mix. On these defaults that is about 17.1 promo days in a 30-day month. A 20-day promo flips ahead of the permanent match by $20.50 ($660.98 vs $640.48). Replace the match price and take rates from your current Seller Center offer.

should-i-offer-two-day-shipping-on-walma.text:
← Walmart Marketplace calculator

Should I offer 2-day shipping on Walmart Marketplace?

Sellers search this after Walmart weights the Buy Box toward two-day delivery. WFS includes that promise after inbound. Buying a 2-day label yourself keeps the listing merchant-fulfilled and eats the faster postage plus pack time. Shipping standard is cheaper on a completed sale and usually converts fewer sessions. The main calculator’s seller-shipping line is one label, so it cannot show whether the 2-day promise is cheaper than WFS.

On the default $24.99 home unit, WFS keeps $4.83 more per session than seller-fulfilled 2-day ($6.92 vs $2.09), $361.94 on 60 WFS units. The $8.95 2-day label and 6 minutes at $18 leave $2.99 on a completed sale — not enough to catch WFS even at 100% take. A $4.50 standard label keeps $9.24 when it sells, but 35% take leaves $3.23. The 2-day label has to fall to about $2.06 before it matches WFS. A $4.50 2-day label with no pack time and matched 80% take flips ahead by $0.47.

Path Take Completed Expected Monthly vs WFS

Expected leftover is take% × completed-sale profit. WFS includes the 2-day promise after inbound and storage. Seller-fulfilled 2-day replaces the WFS pick with the faster label and pack time. Standard shipping uses the cheaper label and a lower take. Complementary to WFS vs seller fulfilled (a completed sale, one label), to returns vs WFS (a refund, not take rate), to aged leftover vs a removal (units already inbound, not take rate), to Walmart Connect vs skip (ad spend, not take rate), and to the price-match view on the main calculator (same take, lower ticket). Paste the labels and take rates from your current Seller Center preview. This page does not publish Walmart’s live fulfillment schedule.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend WFS, a 2-day label, or standard shipping.

Common questions

Should I use WFS or buy a 2-day label myself on Walmart Marketplace?

On the calculator defaults — a $24.99 home unit, 15% referral, standard WFS fulfillment, $1.10 inbound, a $4.50 standard label, an $8.95 2-day label, 6 minutes at $18, 80% WFS take, 70% 2-day take, and 35% standard take — WFS keeps $4.83 more per session than seller-fulfilled 2-day ($6.92 vs $2.09), $361.94 on 60 WFS units. The 2-day label has to fall to about $2.06 before it matches. Standard shipping keeps $3.23 because the cheaper label cannot make up for losing the Buy Box. This page does the arithmetic from the rates you enter; it does not recommend a fulfillment method.

Is Walmart 2-day the same as the WFS versus seller-fulfilled table?

No. The main calculator compares a completed sale on both paths and assumes the offer already won. This page mixes take rate with the faster label and pack time so a cheaper completed-sale leftover does not hide a 2-day Buy Box gap. Price match is a different squeeze: it holds take fixed and drops the ticket.

When does seller-fulfilled 2-day beat WFS?

When the 2-day label plus pack time is cheaper than WFS fulfillment, inbound, and storage, and take stays close. On these defaults a $4.50 2-day label with no pack time and matched 80% take flips ahead by $0.47 per session. Replace the label, minutes, and take rates from your current Seller Center preview.

should-i-pull-aged-wfs-inventory.html.text:
← Walmart Marketplace calculator

Should I pull aged WFS inventory?

Sellers search this after leftover units sit in a Walmart fulfillment center and aged storage starts billing. The main calculator’s WFS vs seller table assumes you are about to inbound a fresh unit, so it cannot show whether pulling a pile that is already there still beats waiting. Inbound, past storage, and cost of goods are already spent. Aged storage is a higher per-cubic-foot rate on what is still sitting.

On the default 40 leftover $24.99 home units, 12% monthly sell-through still leaves a removal $338.35 ahead of keeping them in WFS over 4 months ($599.66 vs $261.31). Disposing loses $14.00. About 16 of the 40 units sell if you wait; the rest keep paying aged storage. Keeping matches if monthly sell-through rises to about 41.3%. At 55% sell-through WFS keeps $55.50 more.

Path Sold Still sitting Carrying Cash vs keep

Keep leftover is monthly sell-through × WFS contribution (sale − referral − pick) minus aged storage on what is still sitting. A removal pays the removal fee, then keeps the seller-fulfilled leftover on every unit. Dispose pays the disposal fee and the units are gone. Inbound, past storage, and cost of goods are sunk. Complementary to WFS vs seller fulfilled (a new inbound), to 2-day vs WFS (take rate), and to returns vs WFS (a sold order that comes back), and to Walmart Connect vs skip (ad spend, not leftover units). Paste the leftover count, aged rate, and removal fee from your current Seller Center preview. This page does not publish Walmart’s live fulfillment schedule.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend a removal, a hold, or a disposal.

Common questions

Should I pull aged inventory out of WFS?

On the calculator defaults — 40 leftover $24.99 home units, 15% referral, standard WFS fulfillment, a $4.50 seller label, $0.50 prep, 12% monthly sell-through, 4 months, $2.10/cu ft aged storage, a $1.25 removal, and a $0.35 disposal — pulling them and selling seller fulfilled keeps $338.35 more than leaving them in WFS ($599.66 vs $261.31). Disposing loses $14.00. Keeping matches if monthly sell-through rises to about 41.3%. At 55% sell-through WFS keeps $55.50 more. This page does the arithmetic from the rates you enter; it does not recommend a removal.

Is the aged WFS table the same as WFS versus seller fulfilled?

No. The main calculator compares a completed sale on a unit you are about to inbound. This page treats inbound, past storage, and cost of goods as already spent, then mixes aged storage on what is still sitting with the leftover you keep if you pull the pile and ship it yourself. Returns are a different mix: a sold order that comes back, not a unit that never sold.

When does leaving aged inventory in WFS still win?

When monthly sell-through is high enough that WFS contribution minus aged storage beats a removal plus your own label. On these defaults that floor is about 41.3%. A 55% sell-through flips WFS ahead by $55.50 over 4 months. Replace the leftover count, sell-through, aged rate, and removal fee from your current Seller Center preview.

should-i-run-walmart-connect-ads.html.text:
← Walmart Marketplace calculator

Should I run Walmart Connect ads?

Sellers search this after Walmart Connect Sponsored Products starts billing last-click sales they already had. The main calculator’s ads-per-unit line is one leftover on a completed sale, so it cannot show whether extra units cover that bill. Skipping ads keeps the organic leftover. Running ads adds extra units and charges ACOS on last-click billed units — a share of organic plus the extras. Spending harder at a higher ACOS buys more extras and usually a larger bill.

On the default $24.99 home unit on WFS, skipping ads keeps $31.15 more than Sponsored Products ($518.99 vs $487.84) on 60 organic units. Twelve extra units at 15% ACOS cannot cover last-click billing on 40% of organic (24 units). Ads match if ACOS falls to about 11.5%, extra units rise to about 18.4, or organic attribution falls to about 26.2%. An 8% ACOS flips ahead by $31.83. A 25% ACOS campaign with 22 extra units and 50% organic attribution leaves $384.42.

Path ACOS Extra units Ad spend Leftover vs skip

Leftover is organic units × completed-sale profit, plus extra ad units × that profit, minus ACOS% × sale price on last-click billed units. Complementary to WFS vs seller fulfilled (a completed sale, one ads line), to 2-day vs WFS (take rate, not ad spend), to returns vs WFS (a refund, not traffic), to aged leftover vs a removal (units already inbound), to the price-match view on the main calculator (same take, lower ticket), and to hold vs match vs promo (Buy Box take on a lower ticket, not ad spend). Paste ACOS, extra units, and attribution from your current Ads Manager report. This page does not publish Walmart’s live ad schedule.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend skipping ads, Sponsored Products, or a higher ACOS.

Common questions

Should I run Walmart Connect Sponsored Products ads?

On the calculator defaults — a $24.99 home unit on WFS, 15% referral, 60 organic units, 12 extra ad units, 15% ACOS, and 40% last-click attribution on organic — skipping ads keeps $31.15 more than Sponsored Products ($518.99 vs $487.84). Ads match if ACOS falls to about 11.5%, extra units rise to about 18.4, or organic attribution falls to about 26.2%. An 8% ACOS flips ahead by $31.83. This page does the arithmetic from the rates you enter; it does not recommend a campaign.

Is Walmart Connect the same as the ads-per-unit line on the main calculator?

No. The main calculator subtracts a flat ads-per-unit leftover from a completed sale and assumes the offer already sold. This page mixes extra units ads buy with last-click billing on a share of the organic sales you already had. A completed-sale WFS versus seller table, a 2-day take-rate mix, a refund mix, and aged leftover are different squeezes.

When do Walmart Connect ads still beat skipping them?

When extra units cover the ACOS bill on last-click attributed organic plus those extra units. On these defaults that is about 11.5% ACOS, 18.4 extra units, or 26.2% organic attribution. An 8% ACOS with the same 12 extra units and 40% attribution flips ahead by $31.83. Replace ACOS, extra units, and attribution from your current Ads Manager report.

should-i-use-wfs-with-walmart-returns.ht.text:
← Walmart Marketplace calculator

Should I stay on WFS after Walmart returns?

Sellers search this after a generous Walmart return policy eats a completed-sale leftover. WFS usually keeps the pick fee and adds return processing. Seller fulfilled already spent the outbound label and then buys a return label plus restock time. Unsellable returns also leave cost of goods on the table. The main calculator’s WFS vs seller table assumes the order stuck, so it cannot show whether returns flip the path.

On the default $24.99 home unit, an 8% return mix still leaves seller fulfilled $0.16 ahead per unit ($7.33 vs $7.17), $9.58 on 60 units. The $2.50 WFS return fee plus a kept $3.95 pick is cheaper than a $4.50 outbound label plus a $5.50 return label, but not enough to wipe a $0.59 completed-sale gap. WFS matches if returns rise to about 11%. At 20% returns WFS keeps $0.49 more and the completed-sale winner flips. A waived WFS return fee flips the 8% mix by $0.04.

Path Completed Return leftover Expected Monthly vs seller

Expected leftover is (1 − return%) × completed-sale profit + return% × return leftover. WFS return leftover keeps the pick fee (unless you mark it refunded) and adds return processing. Seller fulfilled already spent the outbound label, then pays the return label and restock time. Unsellable returns also keep cost of goods. Complementary to WFS vs seller fulfilled (a completed sale) and to 2-day vs WFS (take rate, not a refund), and to aged leftover vs a removal (units that never sold), and to Walmart Connect vs skip (ad spend, not a refund). Paste the return fee and labels from your current Seller Center preview. This page does not publish Walmart’s live fulfillment schedule.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend WFS or seller fulfilled after returns.

Common questions

Do Walmart returns change whether WFS still beats seller fulfilled?

On the calculator defaults — a $24.99 home unit, 15% referral, standard WFS fulfillment, $1.10 inbound, a $4.50 seller label, an 8% return mix, a $2.50 WFS return fee, a $5.50 return label, 8 minutes at $18, and 25% unsellable — seller fulfilled still keeps $0.16 more per unit than WFS after returns ($7.33 vs $7.17), $9.58 on 60 units. WFS matches if returns rise to about 11.0%. At 20% returns WFS keeps $0.49 more and the completed-sale winner flips. This page does the arithmetic from the rates you enter; it does not recommend a fulfillment method.

Is the Walmart returns table the same as WFS versus seller fulfilled?

No. The main calculator compares a completed sale on both paths and assumes the order stuck. This page mixes that leftover with a refunded-order leftover so a cheaper completed-sale path does not hide return processing, the outbound label you already spent, and unsellable units. 2-day take is a different mix: it is Buy Box win versus miss, not a refund.

When do Walmart returns make WFS win?

When the return mix is high enough that WFS return processing plus a kept pick fee beats the outbound label plus a return label. On these defaults that floor is about 11%. A waived $0.00 WFS return fee flips the 8% mix by $0.04. Replace the rate, WFS return fee, and return label from your current Seller Center preview.

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet can price a Walmart listing correctly, and plenty of sellers already have one: sale price times a referral percentage, maybe a fulfillment fee guessed from memory. That formula is exactly right when the SKU is priced well above the referral floor and the only question is the fee on one order. It stops being right the moment either of those changes, and it never answers the six follow-on decisions below.

Walmart charges the larger of the category referral percentage or a fixed per-item minimum — a one-line price × rate formula silently understates the fee on every SKU cheap enough for the floor to bind, which is exactly where margin is already thin. WFS fulfillment is a size-tier step function of dimensions and weight, not a percentage, and storage accrues for however long the unit actually sits. A spreadsheet can model all three correctly — this calculator applies the same method to your own numbers directly, then goes further.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What is the real referral fee on a SKU near the per-item floor? This calculator — it applies max(price × rate, floor), so the floor shows up on its own rather than needing a spreadsheet formula to catch it.
Does WFS or shipping it myself net more on this SKU? This calculator's WFS-vs-seller-fulfilled comparison, including size-tier fulfillment, storage, inbound, and the label you would buy yourself.
Does matching a lower competing offer still leave a profit? This calculator's price-match comparison — a question a fee-only spreadsheet does not model at all.
Do returns, aged inventory, ads, or box size change the answer? This calculator's four follow-on comparisons, run from the same listing inputs. A referral-fee spreadsheet answers none of these.

Nothing here says a spreadsheet is the wrong way to price a Walmart listing — a correctly built one gets the fee right too. The difference is what it costs to keep it right: this calculator applies the referral floor, size-tier fulfillment, and every follow-on decision the same way every time, with no formula to write, extend, or re-check after Walmart's fee schedule changes.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet price a Walmart Marketplace listing correctly?

It can, but the one-line version most sellers start with — sale price times one referral percentage — misses the per-item referral floor that bites cheap SKUs, the WFS size-tier fulfillment fee and storage, and the shipping label cost on a seller-fulfilled order. A spreadsheet can model all of those correctly too, but it has to carry a formula for each one and get the size-tier and floor logic right, and it still stops at the fee — it does not answer whether WFS beats seller fulfilled, whether a price match still leaves a profit, or the other listing-level decisions below.

What does a one-line referral-percentage spreadsheet miss?

The per-item referral floor: Walmart charges the larger of the category percentage or a fixed minimum, so a cheap SKU's real referral fee is the floor, not the percentage — a formula that only multiplies price by rate understates the fee on exactly the listings where margin is already thin. It also misses WFS's size-tier fulfillment fee, which is a step function of dimensions and weight rather than a percentage, and the storage fee for however long the unit sits.

What decisions does this calculator answer that a fee spreadsheet does not?

Whether WFS or shipping the order yourself nets more on this SKU's numbers, whether matching a lower competing offer still leaves a profit, whether a seller-fulfilled 2-day label still beats WFS after take rate, whether WFS still beats seller fulfilled once Walmart's return rate is counted, whether pulling leftover WFS units beats paying aged storage, whether extra Walmart Connect ad spend still covers its own attributed sales, and whether a smaller box crosses a WFS size-tier boundary and cuts the fee. A referral-fee spreadsheet answers none of these; each is a separate comparison this calculator runs from the same inputs.

This calculator vs. Walmart's own WFS Cost Estimator

Walmart publishes its own free fee-estimation tool for sellers inside Seller Center, generally called the WFS Cost Estimator (also shown as an estimated-item-revenue calculator on the inventory page). Walmart's own guide to it is documented at marketplacelearn.walmart.com, and the tool itself is reachable, once signed into a seller account, from seller.walmart.com/wfs/cost-calculator or the calculator icon on the Inventory page's "Manage item" row. It estimates the fulfillment fee, the category referral fee, optional Prep Services, and storage for one WFS item.

That makes it the right tool for one job: the fee Walmart will actually charge to fulfil a specific WFS item right now. It reads Walmart's live schedule, so it is authoritative in a way no third-party page, including this one, can be — referral rates, size-tier fulfillment, and storage vary by category, size, and season, and this site does not publish Walmart's current numbers or claim to. Walmart's own guide also states the estimate does not include inbound shipping or return-processing fees, and that it is an estimate, not a guarantee of actual costs. If you need the current fee for a real listing, that is the tool to open, and this page says so.

wfs-vs-seller-fulfilled.html.text:
← Walmart Marketplace calculator

WFS vs seller fulfilled: which fulfillment path leaves more on the same listing?

Sellers search for “WFS vs seller fulfilled” because the referral fee is not the decision. Both Walmart Fulfillment Services and seller-fulfilled listings usually pay the same category referral percentage — and both can hit Walmart’s per-item referral floor on cheap SKUs. The gap is everything around that.

WFS adds a size-tier fulfillment fee, inbound to a Walmart warehouse, and monthly storage while the unit sits. Two-day shipping is Walmart’s problem after that. Seller fulfilled skips those WFS costs and replaces them with the label, packaging, and time you pay to ship the order yourself.

Walmart listings also get squeezed by a lower offer. Matching that price does not change inbound or your cost of goods — it only shrinks the revenue the referral is taken from. On a typical mid-price example — a $24.99 home unit, 15% referral, a standard WFS fulfillment default, $1.10 inbound, one month of storage, and a $4.50 seller label — one path can keep several dollars more than the other, and a $3 match can wipe the unit out.

Rates change by size tier, season, category, and account. This page does not publish Walmart’s live schedule. Open the Walmart Marketplace calculator, enter the numbers from your current Seller Center preview, and compare both paths on one listing — including the maximum you can pay for the unit and whether a match price still profits. If the decision is the 2-day Buy Box weight rather than a completed sale, use Should I offer 2-day shipping on Walmart? — that page mixes take rate with the faster label. If the order may come back, use Should I stay on WFS after Walmart returns? — that page mixes a refunded-order leftover with the completed sale. If leftover units are already inbound, use Should I pull aged WFS inventory? — that page treats inbound as sunk and compares aged storage to a removal. If the decision is Walmart Connect spend rather than a completed sale, use Should I run Walmart Connect ads? — that page mixes extra units with last-click ACOS on organic sales.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend WFS or seller fulfilled, and it does not claim a listing is profitable after you switch or match.

Common questions

Is WFS or seller fulfilled cheaper on the same listing?

Neither is always cheaper. Both usually pay the same category referral percentage, and both can hit Walmart's per-item referral floor on cheap SKUs, so the decision is everything around that. WFS adds a size-tier fulfillment fee, inbound to a Walmart warehouse, and monthly storage while the unit sits, while seller fulfilled replaces those with the label, packaging, and time you pay to ship the order yourself.

Does matching a lower Walmart offer still leave a profit?

Not always. Matching a lower price does not change inbound or your cost of goods, it only shrinks the revenue the referral is taken from. On a $24.99 home unit at a 15% referral, a $3 match can wipe the unit out. Run the match price through the calculator before you accept it.
